# 04 Storytelling

Status: DRAFT. Tags: [V] repo or platform fact, [H] proposal, [A] assumption to test.

## The unit of story in this game

Situation, decision, cost. A decision card already does this (`docs/WRITING_GUIDE.md` section 5): it names the problem, shows the pressure, and frames the player's decision. The game's central idea is that each choice is paid for somewhere else. A script tells that story in picture and sound.

## What a script must not do

- Tell a hero story. The game is about institutions, constraints and trade-offs. Ben-Gurion and the ministers appear as office-holders making dated, sourced decisions.
- Tell a verdict. The narrator does not say a decision was brave, wise or tragic. The consequence shows it.
- Use suffering as atmosphere.
- Show or imply gameplay that is not in the build (see `08`).

## A story, not a topic

"Water in Israel" is a topic. "In 1951 the prime minister had to choose between continuing drainage works and a complaint from Syria" is a story. A script has a story if a viewer can retell it in two sentences: who faced what problem, what was decided or done, and what it cost or changed.

Check for four things: a setting (who, where, when), a problem with a number or a consequence, a decision or an attempt, and a result. A script that has only a setting and a mood is a montage.

**Picture and voice tell the same story.** If the footage shows a decision card, the voice says what the decision is. A real decision on screen with a voice-over about something else is the most common way a script wastes its best footage.

**No unexplained gaps.** A silent stretch over five seconds needs a reason (a deliberate pause, a title card). Otherwise it is a hole. The checker flags it.

## Beat sheet

| Beat | Job | Typical share |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | One image and at most one line, readable with no sound. Ends on a question or a clear premise. | first 3 seconds |
| Premise | Who you are and when: the prime minister, 15 May 1948. | next 3 to 5 seconds |
| Pressure | The scarcity: money, arms, food, one real constraint with a number. | middle |
| Decision | One real decision card, one real date, the options as the game offers them. Label any counterfactual option. | middle |
| Consequence | The "Why?" panel: what changed and what caused it. | late |
| Honest label | What this footage is: real build, concept art, AI illustration. | on screen, not buried |
| Next step | One verb and one place. | last seconds |

## Shapes

- **6 to 15 seconds, sound off.** Picture-led. One line of on-screen text. For quick-view placements. Steam builds its own 6-second loop from the first video on the page, from six 1-second clips taken at various points (Steamworks, Trailers), so every second of a first video has to stand alone. [V]
- **30 to 60 seconds, explainer.** Premise, pressure, one decision, the Why? panel, the next step.
- **60 to 90 seconds, cinematic.** Only if it is labelled as cinematic and not as gameplay. The existing README trailer is 1:23 and is disclosed as AI-made and not in-game footage. [V]
- **Decision-moment clip, 3.5 to 8 seconds.** Silent. No voice-over. Governed by `docs/event-videos.md`. [V]

## One event per script

Pick at most one real event, dated and sourced, from the game's own event list. The First Truce, the Altalena affair and the Bernadotte assassination are examples the README already names. A script that tours five events explains none of them.

## The archival image comes first

On a decision card the archival photograph comes first and an AI illustration is a switch, labelled (`docs/event-videos.md`). Scripts follow the same order of trust: real footage or archival image, then AI illustration, each labelled. [V as a card rule, H as a script rule]

## Counterfactuals

The game offers options that did not happen. A script says so ("what did not happen") and never shows a counterfactual as history. [V, `docs/event-videos.md`: no footage of what did not happen]

## Endings

A verb and a place: read the sources on GitHub, try the build, report a historical error, help translate. Do not say "coming soon" or "wishlist now" until the thing exists. The Steam page is unpublished (`docs/steam/store-page-draft.md`). [V]

## Timing

Spoken English runs at roughly 150 words a minute, so about 2.5 words a second. [A] The checker uses this to compare the voice-over word count with the time window, and the first recording should replace the assumption with a measured rate.

## Anti-patterns

"In a world...", a countdown, a villain voice, slow motion on suffering, a stack of rhetorical questions, "untold story", a narrator claiming what a real person felt, fake gameplay, music that swells before a fact.
